Because this text is a deeply surreal and visceral piece of prose poetry, "eloquent and professional" can mean two slightly different things depending on your goal. Below are two versions:

* **Option 1: Literary Prose-Poetry (Recommended)** – Refines the punctuation, cadence, and diction to give it an elegant, high-art literary polish while preserving its raw, poetic intensity.
* **Option 2: Formal Narrative Prose** – Restructures the text into a continuous, articulated narrative with standard syntax and sophisticated prose style.

---

### Option 1: High Literary Prose-Poetry

> The redbreast hurls itself repeatedly against the glass until it dies. Inevitably, the blood from its breast will shatter the window into a hundred shards for you to swallow whole. Keep swallowing. 
> 
> The redbreast loves you and demands that you remember this love; thus, it compels you to vomit blindly into the toilet. I was blinded by devotion, drowning in an empty bathtub, spitting up bird droppings, shrouded in crimson feathers.
> 
> • At times, the redbreast indulges in anting—using lit cigarettes, safety pins, and paper cuts. God, how exquisite it feels. It wraps every wound in delicate pink gauze, the exact hue of an artificial sunset. Look: it is a pink soul! It yearns to strip itself bare, yearning for the agony—red teeth, red toes, and mouths agape.
> 
> Who continues to press my head into the sidewalk inside the bathroom? Who keeps the lights burning—the lights that never turn off? Who dissolves upon my tongue? Who takes flight from my finger?
> 
> • The redbreast nests within, positioned behind your left eye and your right, meticulously cleaning its offspring with its beak. It scrubs its babies clean and shakes its tail feathers, scouring the space behind your forehead until it bleeds red. 
> 
> My brain is an edge that cuts. My initials are measured in beats per second, scrubbed down to zero by the rubies in the halo. I whispered your name into the crimson air, and you answered.

---

### Option 2: Formal Narrative Prose

> The redbreast repeatedly sacrifices itself against the windowpane. Sooner or later, the blood within its breast will break the glass into hundreds of pieces for you to swallow whole—and so you continue to swallow. 
> 
> Driven by its love, the redbreast insists that you remember this affection, forcing you to vomit blindly into the toilet. I was completely blinded by love, left drowning in an empty bathtub while spitting up droppings, covered entirely in red feathers.
> 
> • Occasionally, the bird practices anting using lit cigarettes, safety pins, and paper cuts. The sensation is strangely divine. It wraps everything in a pretty pink gauze, matching the shade of a synthetic sunset. Observe: it is a pink soul that desires complete vulnerability and craves the pain—complete with red teeth, red toes, and open mouths.
> 
> I am left asking: who keeps pressing my head into the sidewalk inside the bathroom? Who ensures that the lights remain perpetually on? Who is dissolving on my tongue, and who is taking flight from my finger?
> 
> • The redbreast resides within, stationed behind both your left and right eyes, using its beak to scrub its young clean. It shakes its tail feathers to scour the floor behind your forehead, staining it entirely red. 
> 
> My mind operates like a blade. My identity is reduced to beats per second, scrubbed down to zero by the rubies embedded in the halo. Finally, I whispered your name into the red-tinted air, and you gave me an answer.

outputs.L3:
In this visceral and evocative narrative, the "redbreast" serves not as a traditional harbinger of gentle nature, but as a potent symbol of violent, overwhelming love. This affection is so intense that it transcends emotional turmoil, manifesting instead as acute physical illness, trauma, and profound disorientation. To love, or to be consumed by love in this state, is to be physically dismantled; the speaker experiences passion not as warmth, but as an invasive force that leaves the body reeling and incapacitated.

Crucially, this violent dynamic is not merely endured—it is actively embraced. Affection becomes deeply intertwined with masochism, creating an unsettling space where the narrator derives a dark, paradoxical pleasure from acts of self-harm, physical pain, and bodily destruction. Suffering is recontextualized as a form of devotion, blurring the boundary between torment and tenderness. The speaker finds a strange, ecstatic fulfillment within their own undoing, leaning directly into the forces that shatter them.

As this physical breakdown escalates, the speaker experiences a complete loss of bodily agency. The narrative paints surreal, harrowing portraits of physical vulnerability set against the claustrophobic backdrop of a domestic space. Moments of drowning, violent vomiting, and total physical restraint transform the familiar home into a stage for surreal bodily trauma. Stripped of control over their own form, the speaker becomes a passive subject in a nightmare where the physical frame rebels against itself.

This invasion reaches a terrifying psychological climax as the symbolic bird moves from the external world to take up residence inside the speaker’s mind. Aggressively scouring the dark space behind the eyes, the redbreast systematically hollows out the speaker's consciousness. It picks away at the mind until all rational contemplation is extinguished, effectively reducing the brain's thoughts to zero. In this state of cognitive erasure, the speaker's individual identity is entirely obliterated by the avian manifestation of their passion.

Yet, despite the pervasive violence, sickening bodily distress, and blood-red imagery, the text ultimately resolves with an unexpectedly quiet moment of intimacy. In its final breath, the narrative shifts away from visceral horror toward a soft, transcendent connection. Amidst the ruins of the speaker's physical and mental state, a whispered name breaks through the silence and receives an answer. This simple act of reciprocal recognition reveals the central paradox of the piece: that even within the absolute extremity of destruction, disorientation, and pain, a tender, unbreakable bond remains.
outputs.L4:
It began not with a song, but with a rustle behind the sternum—a wet, frantic fluttering in the dark beneath the ribs. 

At first, I mistook it for devotion. When you spoke my name with that sharp, beautiful cruelty, my heart did not leap; it fractured, and into the fissure flew the redbreast. It was tiny then, a downy thumb of warm blood and needle-thin bones. It roosted in the hollow of my lungs, feeding on the stale air left behind whenever you withdrew your affection. I cultivated it. I thought if I could harbor something so bright and desperate inside me, it would prove that I was capable of loving you with the violence you demanded.

But the bird was never a guest; it was an infection clothed in feathers. 

As the months rotted away, the redbreast grew. Its red throat was not colored by nature, but stained by the slow, continuous leak of my own interior self. It learned the rhythm of my trauma, learning to mimic the precise pitch of your voice when you loved me, and the agonizing silence when you left. To satisfy its appetite, I had to feed it. When your touch turned cold, I used my own hands to carve open pathways for it to stretch. I dragged silver edges across my skin just to give the creature light, mistaking the relief of bleeding for the exorcism of my pain. But the bird only drank the red, grew heavier, and pressed its calcified skull against my inside walls.

It demanded total habitation. 

Every thought of you became a seed of sharp thorn it used to weave its nest. It shredded my memories to line its lair—my childhood, my mother’s voice, the shape of my own face before I met you—all torn into confetti to cushion its weight. The boundaries between your malice, the bird’s hunger, and my own self-loathing dissolved completely. I no longer knew if I was hurting myself to stop the bird from beating its wings, or if the bird was tearing through my sinew to force my hands into violence. My body became a battleground where toxic intimacy wore the mask of a delicate, wild thing, pecking away at the soft tissues of my mind until I was entirely unmade.

In the final days, the song became deafening. It was not music, but a serrated screech echoing through the ribcage it had picked clean. 

The redbreast scoured me from the inside out. It ate the throat that tried to scream; it drank the marrow that held me upright; it swallowed the last quiet corner of my consciousness where a spark of resistance still lived. It scraped the inside of my skull until nothing remained but white dust and hollowed bone. 

Now, there is no "I" left to remember your name, nor a hand left to pull at the skin. There is only the cage, stripped clean and open to the wind. And inside it, sat upon a perch of dry, polished spine, sits the bird—plump, silent, and stained entirely in red—sole survivor of a place that used to be a human being.
outputs.L5:
**The Quiet Presence**

We spend so much of our lives searching for definitive answers—for **the** ultimate truth that will explain the chaos of the world. We look for grand gestures, thunderous revelations, or indisputable signs that point us toward our purpose. 

Yet, **God** rarely speaks in a roar. 

**Sometimes**, the divine is felt in the absolute quiet that follows a storm, when the air settles and the world takes a collective breath. **Sometimes**, it is found in the unexpected kindness of a stranger, or in the quiet resilience of a single flower pushing through a crack in the pavement.

**The** journey of understanding is rarely a straight line defined by constant certainty. It is a slow, unfolding path marked by questions and moments of quiet realization. **Sometimes** we feel deeply connected to the universe, filled with an overwhelming sense of peace. Other times, we wander through the shadows, searching the vast horizon for a hint of direction.

Perhaps **God** is not a distant force waiting to be uncovered at the end of a long search, but the subtle thread of grace weaving through our ordinary days. **Sometimes**, simply pausing to notice those fleeting moments of wonder is enough to remind us that we are never truly alone.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an intense, experimental poem about obsessive love and self-harm, heavily influenced by the style of Richard Siken. Use visceral body horror, frantic line breaks, and central imagery involving a redbreast bird.
counterfactuals.output:
Listen to me. Put down the glass and look at me.
There is a bird inside my sternum, a small red terror 
with a beak like a needle, and it’s digging. It’s digging. 
You said *prove it.* You said *show me the bottom of the room.* 
So I took the razor from the sink—the cold silver, the thin quiet edge—
and I unstitched myself down the center. 
I dragged it down the seam until the skin gave up, 
peeled back like wet wallpaper, bright and steaming 
in the yellow light of the bathroom.

Are you happy now? Is this what you wanted? 

Look at the ribcage parted like a mouth. Look at the redbreast 
thrashing in the meat of my lungs, its feathers slick 
with everything I saved up just to spill on your shoes. 
It’s a robin. It’s small and it’s screaming with my voice. 
It has your name hooked in its tiny, black beak 
and it won't stop pulling at the nerve endings, 
it won't stop weaving the hot red threads of my throat into a nest.

*Don’t look away.* You don’t get to look away. 
I am doing this for you. I am using my thumbs now, 
breaking through the cartilage, prying the bones apart 
so the bird can spread its wings. 

[Say it. Say *I love you* like a punch to the teeth. 
Say *open wider.*]

If I stop digging, the bird dies. 
If I stop bleeding, you’ll put on your jacket and walk out the door. 
So I cut deeper. I carve down past the fat, past the marrow, 
I am making a cave out of my body, I am clearing out the ruin 
so there is room enough for both of us to hide. 

Look at the robin. Its breast is bright, bright crimson—
is it my blood or its own? Does it matter? 
It beats its wet, heavy wings against my spine and I fall to my knees on the linoleum. 
*Sweetheart. My absolute ruin.* 

Put your hand inside me. Don't be gentle. 
Reach past the split bone, touch the bird, feel how fast 
the heart is going. It’s beating for you. It’s dying for you. 
Tell me I’m yours. Tell me to pull out another rib. 
Tell me what else to cut away until there’s nothing left of me 
except the red, and the feathers, and the way I scream your name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

Now, it lives inside the hollow beneath my sternum, building a nursery out of my unspooled nerves and dried pine needles. It does not sleep. When I think of you, it strikes its needle-beak against the interior of my collarbone, a frantic, rhythmic hammering that vibrates up through my jaw until my teeth taste of rust and song. This is how I love you: as a hemorrhage with wings.

It is devouring me from the center out. It eats the soft tissue of my past, swallowing the years before I knew your face like pale, writhing worms, replacing them with a blinding, white-hot devotion that leaves no room for air. My lungs are choked with downy ash. When I try to speak to someone else, my voice is only the sound of eggshells crushing beneath a heavy, invisible foot. 

At night, the bird tilts its head inside my chest, listening to the slow, failing pulse of my heart, deciding it is too quiet, too small for you. So it tears at the muscle, stretching the chamber to fit the terrible magnitude of my longing. Feathers prick the undersides of my skin, pushing through like black splinters. I walk through the world a fragile, hollowed thing—a bone-cage swung from a branch, housing a predator that wears the color of your sweet, unbearable ruin.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark poem about love feeling like a wild bird trapped inside your head that is slowly destroying you from the inside out. Make it feel chaotic and raw.
counterfactuals.output:
You didn’t give me a heart; you slipped a hawk behind my eyes.
A feral, twitching, starve-mad thing
trapped in the calcium cage of my skull,
smashing red-soaked feathers against my temples.

*Flap. Thump. Scritch.*

It thinks my gray matter is wet mud.
It digs.
It gouges deep into the frontal lobe,
shredding my logic to line its nest.
It uses my oldest memories—
my mother’s face, the sound of rain—
as dry twigs, snapping them one by one.
*Crack. Crack. Crack.*

I can’t hear what you’re saying over the screaming.
Not a song. Not a sweet, soft lark.
A wet, guttural shriek that vibrates in my teeth.
It wants *out*.
It wants the open sky of you,
but it only finds parietal bone, hard and unyielding.
So it attacks the walls.

It pecks at my optic nerves—
every time I close my eyes, I see sparks, red and ruined.
It drinks my spinal fluid.
It bathes in my panic.
My thoughts taste like copper and wet down.

You ask me why my hands are shaking.
You ask me why I’m staring at the wall.
*Because it’s fluttering again.*
Because its talons are hooked into my speech center,
snapping the tendons,
turning my voice into a mouthful of loose feathers and rot.

It is growing too big for the vault.
My skull is splintering—
fine, spiderweb fractures behind my forehead.
I can feel the cold air creeping in,
or maybe that’s just my mind leaking out.

Love is not a gentle thing.
Love is a vulture that mistook me for a cage,
and if it ever breaks free,
it will leave only an empty shell,
shattered on the floor,
drenched in blood,
and entirely, hopelessly yours.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

**ALKALINE / PORCELAIN / CARMINE**

the skylight is a scab that won’t stop leaking pigeon chalk.
chalk-spit. 
guano-white drips onto cold linoleum grid—
a slow, calcified baptism of bird shit
mixing with wet pubic curls in the yellow grout.

overhead, a single red bulb hums its violent neon tone.
it paints the room in wet liver.
it paints the walls in arterial rust.

*CRACK.*

the mirror loses its teeth.
glass falls like frozen screaming.
green-bottle shards. silver-backed splinters.
they bite the wet soles of my feet—
tiny razor mouths drinking deep,
spitting back ruby, 
spitting back thick, sugar-beet red.

I am kneeling on the public bathroom floor.
knees grinding into the mosaic of smashed glass and avian bile.
red meets white meets yellow drain-slime.
a swirling, marbleized vomit of flesh and feathers.

and there—
beneath the peeled ribcage,
behind the wet red curtains of my lungs—

is the soul.

it is small. 
it is violently, terribly pink.
a raw-bubblegum ghost.
a boiled-shrimp twitching in the corner by the stall door.
exposed. pastel-naked. 
soft as an unskinned fetus,
gasping against the cold porcelain,
soaking up the glass,
licking the red iron off the floor,
drowning in the pigeon droppings,

and still—
it glows. 
it hums.
a helpless, wet pink tongue
screaming inside the slaughterhouse.
